title: Two American Jacket Giants on Kenyan Trails: North Face vs Columbia Compared
meta_title: North Face vs Columbia: Honest Jacket Picks for 4 Hikes
meta_description: North Face vs Columbia jackets compared: rain tech, warmth, fit and value on Kenyan trails, plus how to buy them thrifted in Nairobi.
excerpt: North Face vs Columbia, compared for Kenyan hikers: how DryVent, FUTURELIGHT, Omni-Tech and Omni-Heat differ, how each brand fits, and which suits Ngong Hills, the Aberdares or Mt Kenya.
content:
North Face vs Columbia is mostly a question of how hard you will push the jacket. The North Face leans technical, with lighter shells and insulation built for wind and altitude, while Columbia gives roomier, warmer-for-the-money layers that suit day hikes around Nairobi. On a thrifted rail, both brands can be excellent value.

Both logos hang side by side on second-hand rails across Kenya at similar prices, so the label alone tells you little; the fabric tag, the cut and the hike matter more. Below we compare rain technology, insulation, sizing and buying tips, then match each brand to real Kenyan trails.

Quick Facts

  • Origins: Columbia began in Portland, Oregon, in 1938; The North Face opened in San Francisco in 1966.
  • Rain tech: The North Face uses DryVent and FUTURELIGHT; Columbia uses Omni-Tech and OutDry Extreme.
  • Warmth tech: The North Face relies on down and ThermoBall synthetic fill; Columbia adds Omni-Heat reflective dots to many linings.
  • Fit: Columbia generally cuts roomier; The North Face labels most styles Slim, Standard or Relaxed.
  • Short answer: In North Face vs Columbia, pick The North Face for altitude and Columbia for value on day hikes.
  • Kenyan seasons: Short rains run roughly October to December and long rains roughly March to May.

North Face vs Columbia: Which Is Better for Kenyan Hikers?

Neither brand wins outright. The North Face is the stronger pick for high, cold, windy mountains and for the lightest packable layers. Columbia is the better buy for day hikes, wet forest trails and maximum warmth per shilling.

That split follows their roots: Columbia grew from a family hat business into practical, generously cut outerwear, while The North Face began as a climbing shop. A typical North Face shell feels lighter and trimmer in the hand.

How Do Their Rain Jackets Compare?

On rain protection, North Face vs Columbia comes down to where the membrane sits. The North Face hides its membrane behind a face fabric, while Columbia's top shells put the membrane on the outside so there is nothing to soak.

What is DryVent?

DryVent is The North Face's everyday waterproof fabric: a breathable polyurethane coating, a durable water-repellent (DWR) finish and fully taped seams. It comes in 2-layer (with a mesh or insulated lining), lighter 2.5-layer and tougher 3-layer builds, as The North Face's DryVent page sets out.

What makes FUTURELIGHT different?

FUTURELIGHT, launched in January 2019, is sprayed through thousands of tiny nozzles to form a porous web rather than a solid film. The brand told Outside Business Journal that it passes 1-2 CFM of air, against 0.01-0.1 CFM for most waterproof jackets.

What are Omni-Tech and OutDry Extreme?

Omni-Tech is Columbia's multilayer waterproof-breathable fabric, used on most of its rain shells, including the Watertight and Arcadia jackets. OutDry Extreme is the clever one: Columbia describes it as an external membrane bonded to a soft lining, so the outside never wets out and goes heavy.

Which works better in the short rains?

For a three-hour forest walk in November, an Omni-Tech or DryVent 2-layer jacket is plenty. For a long wet day on Elephant Hill, where rain can last for hours, OutDry Extreme or a 3-layer DryVent or FUTURELIGHT shell holds up better, so the North Face vs Columbia call here depends on the model more than the badge. Pair either with waterproof rain pants, and see our guide to rain jackets for Nairobi hikers for shell checks.

Which Brand Keeps You Warmer at Altitude?

For a dry, cold summit push, a North Face down jacket gives the best warmth for its weight. For damp cold or a tighter budget, Columbia's Omni-Heat-lined jackets are the better North Face vs Columbia call for the price.

ThermoBall vs Omni-Heat

ThermoBall is a synthetic fill The North Face developed with PrimaLoft; its round fibre clusters copy the way down traps air, and the brand says it keeps insulating when wet. Omni-Heat is not a fill at all. Columbia prints reflective dots onto the lining, silver on the older Omni-Heat Reflective and gold on Omni-Heat Infinity, to bounce body heat back while sweat vapour escapes between them. That sums up North Face vs Columbia insulation: one engineers the fill, the other the lining.

What about down?

Both brands sell down jackets, but The North Face offers more at the high end, from the boxy Nuptse to Summit Series pieces. Down packs smallest, which helps when your porter bag on Mt Kenya has a weight limit; keep it in a dry bag, because wet down loses its loft. In a North Face vs Columbia contest for summit warmth per gram, this is where The North Face pulls ahead. For layering ideas, see our cold-weather layering guide.

Do the Two Brands Fit the Same?

No. Columbia generally runs roomier, so many hikers drop half a size or a full size. The North Face cuts closer and prints a fit label (Slim, Standard or Relaxed) on most styles, so check it before choosing.

Whichever side of North Face vs Columbia you lean, remember both are American brands, so a Medium from either is usually bigger than a Medium from a European label. Try any jacket on over the fleece you hike in, lift both arms and check that the hem stays below your belt and the sleeves still cover your wrists when you reach forward.

North Face vs Columbia on Four Kenyan Hikes

The right brand changes with the trail. Here is our North Face vs Columbia pick for four common hikes from Nairobi.

  1. Ngong Hills in the short rains: Ridge wind and showers. A Columbia Omni-Tech shell with a mesh lining is comfortable and affordable. See our Ngong Hills hike guide.
  2. Mt Longonot on a hot, dusty day: You mostly carry the jacket, so a light North Face DryVent 2.5L or FUTURELIGHT shell that rolls into a 28L day backpack wins on weight.
  3. Elephant Hill or Table Mountain in the Aberdares: Long, cold, wet days. Columbia OutDry Extreme or a 3-layer North Face shell over a fleece.
  4. Point Lenana on Mt Kenya (4,985 m): A 2:00-3:00am start below freezing. A North Face down or ThermoBall jacket under a hard shell, plus Thinsulate waterproof gloves. Our Mt Kenya hiking guide explains summit night.

The higher and longer the hike, the more the lighter technical pieces pay off. For the weekend hills within two hours of Nairobi, Columbia's value is hard to beat, and that is the honest summary of North Face vs Columbia for most local hikers.

How Should You Buy Thrifted North Face or Columbia in Nairobi?

Buy the jacket, not the logo. Read the fabric tag, test the zips, check the seam tape and look at wear points before you pay. A good second-hand shell from either side of the North Face vs Columbia divide can give years of use for a fraction of the new price.

What should you check on a used jacket?

Run your fingers along the seam tape at the shoulders and hood; peeling tape means leaks. Pull every zip end to end, including pit zips. Then splash a little water on the shoulder: if it beads, the DWR still works; if it soaks in, the jacket needs washing and re-proofing, not binning. The same checks apply on both sides of the North Face vs Columbia choice.

How do you tell genuine from a copy?

Look for even stitching on the logo, an inner care label with fabric content and a style code, and smooth branded zip pulls. No single sign is proof, so judge the whole jacket.

Pro Tips

  • In any North Face vs Columbia decision, read the inner tag first: DryVent, FUTURELIGHT, Omni-Tech or OutDry tells you more than the logo.
  • Wash shells after dusty murram trails and every wet hike; dust and sweat clog membranes faster than rain does.
  • Revive the DWR with a technical wash and low-heat tumble, and keep shells out of strong sun when not in use.
  • Wear merino hiking socks and a wicking base layer; no shell can fix a sweat-soaked cotton T-shirt.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Columbia as good as North Face for hiking?

Columbia matches The North Face for most Kenyan day hikes, and often costs less. Its Omni-Tech and OutDry Extreme shells keep out heavy rain, and Omni-Heat linings feel very warm. The North Face pulls ahead on light, packable pieces for high mountains, especially down jackets and FUTURELIGHT shells. Choose by the trail, not the badge.

North Face vs Columbia for Mt Kenya: which one should I take?

For Mt Kenya, The North Face has the edge on summit night because its down and ThermoBall jackets pack small and give strong warmth for their weight. A Columbia Omni-Heat jacket still works if it fits under your shell. Layer it: base layer, fleece, insulated jacket and waterproof shell.

North Face vs Columbia sizing: does Columbia run big?

Columbia usually runs bigger than The North Face, especially through the chest and waist, so many people size down by half or a full size. The North Face varies by style, which is why it prints Slim, Standard or Relaxed fit labels. Always try a jacket on over the fleece you plan to hike in before deciding.

Are North Face and Columbia jackets really waterproof?

North Face DryVent and FUTURELIGHT jackets and Columbia Omni-Tech and OutDry Extreme jackets are fully waterproof when new, with taped seams. Many fleeces and softshells are only water-resistant, so check the tag. On used jackets, peeling seam tape and a tired DWR finish are the usual causes of leaks.

Can I find original North Face or Columbia in Nairobi?

Yes, original North Face and Columbia jackets turn up regularly on Nairobi's second-hand market, including at our Mountain Mall shop on Thika Road. Whatever your North Face vs Columbia leaning, check the care label, style code, stitching and zips. Stock changes weekly, so WhatsApp us before you visit.

Final Thoughts

Light North Face shells and down jackets earn their keep above 3,500 m, while Columbia's roomier, warmer-for-the-money layers suit the hills and craters around Nairobi. Settle your own North Face vs Columbia question by reading the fabric tag and trying the jacket on over your fleece, then pick one up before the short rains settle in.
